attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the antecedent (OpenAI can't pay its bills) and renders 'it's fucked' fairly as severe trouble. 'Fucked' is firm language, not a hedge. The leverage premise is background to the conditional.

contract.note: Reading the antecedent as a material payment failure, and the consequence as default, distressed restructuring or loss of investment-grade financing, is an ordinary plain reading. No deadline is supplied, and the contract handles that correctly.

evidence.note: Oracle's FY2026 release documents $43B of debt raised and $75B in prepaid or customer-supplied hardware. It says nothing about any OpenAI payment failure, so the antecedent is not shown.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast with no deadline. The packet has no documented OpenAI payment failure by the evaluation date, so the antecedent's status is unknown and no conclusive event has occurred. Under policy the claim cannot be scored yet. Oracle's financing figures are background only.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. He cites no one else for the $2T figure in this passage.

semantics.note: The proposition is faithful. The conditions field is garbled: its 'antecedent' text mixes the consequent into the antecedent. The real antecedent is a shortfall below $2T of new revenue by 2030. The claim works more as a conditional necessity than as a prediction that the revenue will be earned.

contract.note: The contract correctly says this is not a prediction that $2T will be earned, and it flags the annual-versus-cumulative and baseline ambiguities. Taking 'by 2030' to mean the end of 2030 is generous to the speaker but makes no difference now.

evidence.note: Bain's 2025 model of about $2T in annual revenue needed by 2030. It is a scenario with a wider scope, not evidence of a realised outcome.

reviews.rationale: The horizon runs to 2030, after the evaluation date. Neither the revenue shortfall nor the claimed allocation of benefits can be known yet, and no decisive early event appears in the packet. The Bain model is context only.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The proposition is a faithful present-tense observation linking a share of at least 50% to roughly $748B. Neither the hyperscaler set nor the accounting basis is stated.

contract.note: Putting Oracle in the hyperscaler set is the evaluator's choice. The surrounding text treats hyperscalers as Microsoft, Google and Amazon, and discusses Oracle separately. With Oracle included, the packet's figures put total RPO above $1.7T, which makes '$748B and at least 50%' arithmetically impossible. So the result turns on an unsupplied reading.

evidence.note: Microsoft: about 45% of $625B RPO came from OpenAI at December 2025. Earlier snapshot, one supplier, one lab.
Microsoft's RPO was $627B at March 2026, with no dollar figure attributed to OpenAI or Anthropic.
Alphabet's RPO was $467.6B at March 2026, with no attribution to the two labs.
Oracle: $638B RPO and $75B prepaid or customer-supplied hardware. Neither figure is attributed to the two labs.

reviews.rationale: No customer-level attribution of OpenAI and Anthropic RPO across hyperscalers is in the packet. Amazon's RPO is missing. Whether the share is at least 50% depends on whether Oracle counts as a hyperscaler, and the speaker did not say. The evidence cannot settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, inside a rhetorical passage about data centres.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'appears' and the Claude uptime exception. But 'appears' marks an impression held at graded confidence, not a firm assertion, and the drafter itself calls both parts hedged.

contract.note: The contract applies a plain reading by treating 'appears' as a firm claim about public evidence. Plain readings apply only to firm language. Its choice of period and its reading of 'improve products' to include usage limits are also the evaluator's own.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own disclosure dated May 6, 2026. It says compute deals let it double Claude Code limits and remove peak-hour reductions. On its face this cuts against the claim, but it is the company's own account and is not scored here.

reviews.rationale: Both limbs are hedged with 'appears', which signals an impression rather than a firm commitment, and they sit in a rhetorical passage. Under policy, hedged language is not scored. Anthropic's May 2026 limit increases would cut against a firm version of the second limb.
